## 1. Movies where criminals unknowingly mess with the wrong guy?

**Score:** 68
**Body:** Hey guys, do you know any movies with this kind of vibe?

Criminals unknowingly kidnap or kill the child/family member of a mafia guy, corrupt cop, ex-criminal, or some powerful guy who has done some bad things in the past. Then that guy goes absolutely hard, using all the connections, power, influence, and shady people he has to hunt them down.

Basically, **the criminals picked the worst possible person to mess with**, and it's super satisfying watching him tear through everyone standing in his way.

## 3. Movies where someone travels far away to live in an isolated mansion for a while?

**Score:** 19
**Body:** Looking for movies with a very specific vibe: a character has to travel a long distance (car, train, bus, whatever) to some remote mansion/estate/huge old house, usually for work, family, an inheritance, caretaking, etc., and actually stays there for some time.

I especially want the in-between stuff: arriving somewhere unfamiliar, settling into a room, wandering around the property, exploring rooms they probably shouldn't, boring evenings, meals, routines, discovering the surrounding area, slowly getting to know the house/people there.

It doesn't have to be horror or even mysterious. Drama, romance, thriller, comedy, gothic, supernatural... anything works. The isolation, travel, temporary life in a big unfamiliar house is what I'm after.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Tony (2026) script was a disservice to Bourdain

**Score:** 307
**Body:** Nothing against Matt Johnson. This seems to be a case of a great director rescuing a mediocre script, which apparently started out as a Blacklist screenplay.

The writers obviously read *Kitchen Confidential* enough to include some details from it, but misunderstood the point of the book.

Anthony Bourdain's whole rise to fame was built on challenging the romantic ideal of professional cooking. *Confidential* showed that kitchens weren't the white-apron artists' studios that diners would like to imagine. His whole argument was that professional cooks deserve respect because they're essentially blue-collar food mechanics: overworked; underpaid; burnt out; self-medicating to deal with the stress, going through hell and back every shift, and *still* (usually) managing to turn out great food for other people.

That whole thesis should have showed up in the Chef's character and his relationship with Tony.

Instead, we got the "old master seeing some ineffable genius in a flawed apprentice" cliche, the exact kind of romanticism that the real-life Bourdain made his name by exposing as a fairy tale.

If the whole point was that Banderas's character failed because he was too much of a romantic, that should have come out more consistently in the dialogue. He should have been telling Tony that he wasn't ready for the white coat until he proved he could be a good soldier, that he *wasn't* too much of an idealist. Not handing him the damn thing as soon as his training started.

Tony trying to talk him into making a complicated special should have been another deal-breaker. Somebody in the Chef's position should have known firsthand that nobody's there to make art—certainly not the new guy. A "special" is something used to dress up stuff that needs to get moved before it goes bad. A "signature dish" is a featured menu item that is carefully planned, from ingredients to staffing to preparation, before a customer ever sees it. It's something you rehearse ahead of time to make sure it won't fuck up your service, and it's *not something you give to the new guy to prove himself.*

Burning down the kitchen should have been the end of the relationship. That's unequivocal proof that Tony didn't have what it actually takes to work in a kitchen. It's why you have to earn your way onto the line one step at a time in real life. No amount of hidden genius makes up for not knowing your place on the team and holding the line. Your aesthetic appreciation for the food isn't enough to save you. *Discipline* is the only quality that matters. You're either pulling the oars with everybody else, or you're a liability. No recommendation letter. No second chance. You put yourself before the restaurant, you're done.

I know they had that line about "I trusted you, and that's the problem." But it should never have been a matter of trust. Professional kitchens have strict norms and protocols precisely because they're crewed by burned-out degenerates. Ignoring those protocols doesn't make sense from somebody who, we're told, was once one of the elites.

Ironically, there would have been an interesting parallel to drawn between professional cooking and professional writing. Neither tolerates romanticism for long. Idealists show up expecting to be recognized for their genius. In both trades, the old pros know that you only succeed by grinding it out for years before you earn your keep; the reward is getting to keep rolling the same boulder up the same hill, over and over, until you get old or quit, and maybe stealing a few moments of glory along the way.

Solid movie overall. I don't think Bourdain would have objected to the way *he* was portrayed in the film. But he might have taken issue with the way the industry was presented, given that he wrote one of the most famous books to demystify it.

The movie is only adapting like...two early chapters of Kitchen Confidential where he largely revels in the pirate lifestyle of him and his fellow crew. It's one snapshot in time, I don't think it was ever going to encapsulate the issues that the book really delves into when Bourdain is fully down in the dumps about his own career and the life. 


2. sorry this isn’t a really super deep response but i was watching some interviews with the cast, and in one of them after speaking with matt and dominic the interviewer video-calls antonio banderas to ask about his process with the character and he spent literally 25 straight minutes yapping about how great all his restaurants are IRL and how he’s the most epic restaurant owner ever and i thought that was really funny

they should've put Clancy Brown in that role.

"i need a *half* dozen *Well*fleets! *Fuck!*"
3. Very good point and frankly describes what I felt the movie was missing. It was there in terms of ambiance/environment, like refusing to show the other chefs “wowed” by Tony, but the film didn’t quite show why he worked hard (except for the girl) and/or what he realized about cooking in the end. It felt more of a redemption arc more than a character origins arc.  
  - i wrote in another comment on a different post that they could easily have cut the love story out after the first act. they had all the pieces in place to show Tony getting hooked on the rush.

i spent about a decade in the industry, and what kept me going was the high you get when everything clicks in the midst of the chaos. that's part of why the kitchen attracts so many masochists with substance issues: it's an extreme sport that happens to pay in cash, and has a full bar on-site.

i think that explains Bourdain's story much better than a contrived romance plot.
4. I have not seen this movie yet but did really enjoy your perspective in this post.

The idea of Bourdain as a culinary genius at the start of a journey to realize his full potential is ridiculous. He was a famously great chef, but the 'genius' aspect of his life and work was his ability to interpret and communicate. Like how a lawyer can read volumes of dense legislation and cases and come back with simple and succinct information and recommendations for a client; Bourdain's unique role (at the Kitchen Confidential stage of his career) was accurately interpreting and translating all of the dark, hilarious, surreal, and practical things about life in the industry and communicating it to broader audiences. In fact, he was so good at it that his later work as a tv host had him doing that on a global scale by making observations about history/culture/politics around the world using food as a both a show-running conceit and as a gateway/medium for delving into those topics.

Anyways. I was reluctant to see the movie because I find that noone has been as capable of telling Bourdain's story better than he was when he was alive. But Sessa was great in The Holdovers and I really enjoy Matt Johnson's work, so I do intend to check it out, but am also grateful I read this beforehand.
  - I do not think they portray him as anything even remotely near a culinary genius in this movie, even by the end. He’s just a fuck up trying/failing to be a writer. 
    - Yeah that's what rings hollow or untrue about a lot of the criticism i'm reading in this thread. It doesn't deify Bordain at all, he's an asshole and a compulsive liar that at the end actually starts making efforts to learn to cook. It's not a romantic ideal of him at all.

## 2. The horror in "Rosemary's Baby" hit me deeper when I focused on Ruth Gordon's genre-defying performance

**Score:** 72
**Body:** I’m rewatching some horror classics lately and noticing that many of my old favorite include supporting characters whose plots seem written for a different genre. As in: Toni Collette doesn’t know she is in a horror movie in “The Sixth Sense”; if we only watch the scenes she is in – until her last one, at least –, we’d be watching a drama about an overworked single mother who’s struggling to raise a child with deep, undiagnosed psychological issues.

Now, after seeing “Rosemary’s Baby” for the first time in 20 years, I found the same can be said about Ruth Gordon’s Oscar-winning performance as Mia Farrow’s neighbor. The role was not written with the comic relief intent that we got from some of Aunt Gladys’s scenes in “Weapons”, but Gordon’s register is fully comedic in essence.

About 30 minutes into the movie, we get the confirmation that she is running a satanic cult with her husband and trying to impregnate Rosemary with the devil’s child, but even her brief remark during the ritual can make one chuckle. And in the next scenes, we’re never really scared of her personally; we are creeped out by the knowledge of what she's capable of doing one night and then stopping by for tea the next day. And keep being mostly annoyed by the character’s nosiness and intrusiveness. This is a lady who won't let you refuse an unsolicited dessert.

Unlike Collette’s struggling mom, Gordon’s New Yorker old broad KNOWS she is in a horror movie. She just doesn’t care - and that's where the humor and the real creeps come from. The movie’s atmosphere relies on this woman’s indifference to the supernatural events happening around her and for the role she played on it - to the very final scene, when Rosemary finds her way into the neighbor’s apartment to learn the shocking truth, Gordon’s attitude is still in the lines of “oh, it’s just you, Rosemary”.

That's a fantastically well-written character and performance.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. And what I really love about her, her husband and the coven is this ordinary setting. They’re not powerful, not rich or influential. They’re not even regular people, but the typical a tiny bit weird (in German a bit spießig, in French Petite bourgeoisie, I don’t know the right word in English) and more than never annoying neighbors you can end up wit in a city like New York. 
  - What is somewhat delicious about the whole thing is that one of the more clean readings of Rosemary's Baby is that this entry into the urban, "modern" Middle Class is itself somewhat Satanic. A young couple who gets into a "good" building slightly above their means.
  - They're rich though. It's a very nice apartment building they move into.
  - Petty bourgeois would probably be the right term in English. Obviously much like the French but with the added connotation that they are annoyingly concerned with minor things.
2. I think you've denoted very well some of what makes *Rosemary's Baby* a real classic. I can't watch many horror movies, they frighten me too much, but *Rosemary's Baby* (thankfully) creates an atmosphere of dismal horror rather than pure shock-scare-overwhelm. 

(I suppose it's a bit like *Get Out* in that way?)

Rosemary's Baby has that wonderful pedestrian-conspiracy-horror angle to it. No one person is more complicit than another—except, perhaps, the husband—and that's part of what makes it so terrifying. It's not a mindless and nameless horror, it's not Voldemort or Darth Vader; instead it's a small conspiracy that has completely taken over this woman's life. 

Honestly I'm sort of surprised this film hasn't been brought up in the modern Epstein files discourse, because the movie does, quite compellingly, portray a malicious cabal as just slightly outside the bounds of normalcy, not absconded in an evil lair, but living right next to you, the couple who you easily mistook for doting pensioners. 
3. Her character isn't INDIFFERENT, she's projecting an extremely specific and well-crafted persona to DISARM Rosemary or anyone around her, including the audience. Nearly every moment they are on screen they are 100% dedicated to that illusion, and it's only briefly broken in a few moments (particularly Minnie scolding Laura-Louise near the end.)

Anton LaVey, founder of the Church of Satan, was an on-set subject expert for the film and he helped inform Polanski on how the Castevets would go about their lives manipulating people-- in Satanism its called *Satanic Lesser Magic*.

There are three main flavors of lesser magic someone can depend on: arousal (sexuality), intrigue (mystery), and sentimentality (comfort), and each Magician has to decide what and how much of each to employ to their best abilities. 

As elderly individuals arousal is pretty much unavailable and intrigue wouldn't lure Rosemary in (but it did for Guy in the form of a mysterious meeting about his career), so sentimentality is what they employ. The Castavets do their absolute best to be the kind, nurturing elderly neighbors who never had children of their own whenever they are around Rosemary.

Additionally, Mimmie's quirkiness layer helps to further disarm by making Rosemary second guess every red flag interaction she has with them, and once they have Guy involved he can gaslight her and absorb any relationship blowbacks that would otherwise drive a wedge between Rosemary and Castavets.
  - Everything you say seems right and germane enough \[edit in: but, several Internet sources say that the Anton LaVey involvement is a **false** legend of the film, he was **not** involved\], but I think in the film the effect is more than this. There is an implicit critique of ascending to the modern Middle Class in this film. So, not only is Ruth's harmless Old neighbor act effective at disarming Rosemary, there is also the implicit idea that the more "normal" ambitions of a young couple, to career climb, to get into a "good" building, to have a baby, themselves are "Satanic". Not that they "hide" Satanism (which certainly is the case in the film), but also that they HAVE a darkness and manipulation in themselves. Its a critique of consumer Capitalism, just like how we see Guy in a motorcycle commercial selling a lifestyle. As Guy stops paying attention to his young lovely wife, concentrating on his career, giving attention to those who would empower him, putting it upon the wife to then have a baby, somewhat all on her own, isolated, this is also just everyday "normal" stuff...
  - >Anton LaVey, founder of the Church of Satan, was an on-set subject expert for the film and he helped inform Polanski on how the Castevets would go about their lives manipulating people-- in Satanism its called Satanic Lesser Magic.

Weird that they wouldn't choose a Theistic Satanist. The themes and events portrayed in the movie are Theistic satanism, and are not really compatible with Lavey's non-theistic Church of Satan, who are prescriptively atheists.
  - Of course she has a plan; I meant she is indifferent to the harm she is causing this woman, and not once showing a hint of other side (think Ann Dowd in Hereditary if we remove the scenes where her character displays her true devotion).
4. You hit the Gordon performance nail on the head...other than one small thing for me, I didn't find it funny much at all. I've watched the film many times, and she really is amazing. Only that one small moment in the drugged rape scene when she changes her tone into a authoritative and controlling (asserting something like "If she ate the chocolate mouse there is nothing to worry about!") is she a bit frightening, like the whole old lady act is actually something of an act, a brilliant touch by Polanski. Maybe if I think about it moments of her performance are funny, like when the two neighbors sit down with their knitting on the new couch, and clearly the couple find her funny in the beginning. I just didn't find humor there. Maybe a kind of endearing bemusement?

Not saying you are wrong at all, just offering a different experience of the film, a bit. A great post!

## 3. Directors Whose Earlier Work Makes You Look at Them in a Completely Different Light?

**Score:** 32
**Body:** My first exposure to the films of Jonathan Demme was THE SILENCE OF THE LAMBS (1991) and PHILADELPHIA (1993). As such, I had thought of him as the maker of serious dramas (Having later watched his BELOVED \[1998\] and RACHEL GETTING MARRIED \[2008\] didn't change my opinion).

But a few months ago I finally watched Demme's SOMETHING WILD (1986), which I loved. Admittedly, the finale of that film was violent and suspenseful enough to make me say, "If I were a studio exec who was thinking of adapting the novel SILENCE OF THE LAMBS, those scenes I just watched would have convinced me Demme could handle stuff like Hannibal Lecter's escape."

What I didn't expect was how wacky both SOMETHING WILD and MARRIED TO THE MOB (1988), which I literally saw for the first time last night, are and just how adept Demme seemed to be at directing comedy (offbeat, dark, physical, etc). Those two movies, which are both currently available to stream on Criterion Channel, completely opened my eyes.

Has anyone had a similar experience watching a different filmmaker's earlier output and, if so, which director? Specifically, you had previously thought of them as strictly making movies of a particular sort, but subsequently realized they were more versatile than you had originally thought?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Verhoeven. Never would've thought the RoboCop/Total Recall/Starship Troopers guy would have been making such excellent horny euro art cinema as Turkish Delight.

Showgirls and Basic Instinct feel more subversive and less trashy after going through his 70s stuff as well.
  - Yeah I actually think Basic Instinct is a very well directed film. The cinematography choices especially are top notch

## 5. Some thoughts about Spike Jonze's "Her" and Samantha's ability to love

**Score:** 8
**Body:** Rewatching the movie, I got the impression that the AIs never really get to experience "emotions" like we do. They just go from point A – emulating human behavior – to point B – an evolutionary process - after studying and analyzing the humans emotions that drive such behaviors and that the computer programs couldn't possibly "feel".

As in: at first, it's clear that Samantha is highly sophisticated at imitating human patterns. We see this in her first sexual interaction with Theodore, when she moans and make sounds that would require the physical sensations of a body to be produced. Her awkwardness the next morning also comes across as learned behavior: she recognizes how humans commonly behave after sex and knows enough about Theodore to conjure an appropriate emotional response.

But throughout the movie, Samantha – who, and that’s important, begins as a program designed to assist Theodore in his daily life - continuously researches everything available on human emotions, relationships, and experiences to tend to Theodore's emotional needs. That's what she must do after he relies on her for romantic companionship. That leads to Samantha and other AI - also used by other people for emotional support - forming their own unique concepts of feelings and relationships.

Those concepts are not understandable to humans. AI and people are fundamentally incompatible. As in: when Theodore discovers that Samantha is simultaneously involved with hundreds of other people, we understand that the time a person must dedicate of their finite lives to another person that they love was removed from Samantha's equation. Her "love" didn't come with sacrifice. She was expanding her informational networtk.

When the AIs leave, they seem to have evolved into something humans can no longer relate to. Samantha says so at the end – “love was different for them”; but it was only this time around that I realized "love" was ALWAYS different for them; it never evolved from AI actually experiencing human love for themselves. That's all to say that only the people in the movie are experiencing love as we know it.
